Autumn 2025

Equations

  • Mathematics allows us to model the world using equations.

  • E.g.,

    • probability distributions,
    • progression of disease through a population,
    • explosive force over distance,
    • exchange rate of currencies,
    • trajectory of a ball through the air.

  • Generally, we can process more information visually than by looking at numbers and symbols.

\[ f(x)=\frac {1}{\sqrt {2\pi \sigma^2}} e^{-{\frac {(x-\mu )^2}{2\sigma^2}}} \]

Linear algebra

  • In this session, we will focus on linear equations and vectors,

    a simple but powerful model.

  • Models “flat” objects (points, lines, planes) in space.

  • Useful in, among many others, computer graphics and vision, data analysis, machine learning, quantum physics…

  • The more general concept of matrices and vectors can be applied even more widely (to non-flat objects)

  • For every linear equation (or system), there is a corresponding picture.

  • Granted, sometimes the picture might be in \(42\)-dimensional space…

Equations

  • mathematical formula (usually cantaining unknows variables) with an equality.

    • \(5x^2 - 3x + 4 = 0\)
    • \(e^{a^2} + \tfrac{1}{a} = 4\)
    • \(3y + 2z = 4w + y\)
    • \(c = 5\)

Solutions to equations

  • A solution is a value, which can be assigned to an unknown variable to make the equality true.

    • For example, \(x^2 = 9\)
    • when \(x = 3\), we have \(3^2 = 9\) and \(x = -3\), we have \((-3)^2 = 9\),
    • \(3\) and \(-3\) are solutions to \(x^2 = 9\).

  • Sometimes we specify the number set for our solutions

    • The equation \(y^2 = 3\) has solutions \(\pm \sqrt{3}\) – two real solutions but no rational or integer solutions.
    • The equation \(z^2 = -1\) has no real solutions, but does have solutions over complex numbers.

demonstrate graphs in desmos

Linear equations

\[ a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + \cdots + a_n x_n = b \]

  • In any number of unknown variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\),

  • Variables multiplied by a real number (\(a_1,\ldots,a_n, b\)),

  • Solutions in real numbers.

  • no fractions, powers or special functions (e.g., \(\sin\), \(\log\))

  • For example

    • \(x + 1 = 3\)
    • \(2x + 3y = 4\)
    • \(\frac{1}{4} x_1 + \frac{13}{19}x_2 + \frac{12}{19} x_3 = \frac{pi}{2}\)

note, in the last equation: 1) you can multiply everything by a real number to clear the fractions, 2) constants can be any real number, even irrational ones.

Systems of linear equations

\[ \begin{align*} a_{11}x_{1}+a_{12}x_{2}+a_{13}x_{3}+\cdots a_{1n}x_{n}=&b_{1}\\a_{21}x_{1}+a_{22}x_{2}+a_{23}x_{3}+\cdots a_{2n}x_{n}=&b_{2}\\\vdots&\\a_{m1}x_{1}+a_{m2}x_{2}+a_{m3}x_{3}+\cdots a_{mn}x_{n}=&b_{m} \end{align*} \]

  • A related collection of one or more (\(m\) here) equations in one or more (\(n\) here) unknowns.
  • A solution \(x_1=c_1, x_2=c_2,\ldots,x_n=c_n\) is an assignment of real numbers to variables which makes all equations true.

Two equations in two unknowns

\[ \begin{align*} 3x_{1}+5x_{2}=&9\\x_{1}-x_{2}=&1 \end{align*} \]

Flashbacks to algebra in school…

  • Multiply second equation by \(3\) to get \(3x_1 - 3x_2 = 3\)
  • Subtract this from the first: \(8x_2=8 \Longrightarrow x_2 = 1\).
  • We can use \(x_2=1\) to solve for \(x_1\) by substituting it in:
  • \(x_1 - (1) = 1\Longrightarrow = 1 + 1 = 2\)
  • Solutions: \(x_1 = 2, x_2 = 1\).

This method can be generalised to any number of equations in any number of unknowns. - One of the most efficient methods of solving large linear systems (complexity \(\mathcal{O}(n^3)\)), called Gaussian Elimination.

Two equations in two unknowns

\[ \begin{align*} 3x_{1}+5x_{2}=&9\\x_{1}-x_{2}=&1 \end{align*} \]

One might prefer to draw a picture…

  • Each straight line represents one equation
  • The intersection point is the solution to the system.

Possibilities

\[ \begin{align*} a_1 x_1 + b_1 x_2 &= c_1\\ a_2 x_1 + b_2 x_2 &= c_2\\ \end{align*} \]

  1. Unique solutions: lines intersect in a unique point,
  2. No solutions: lines are parallel and never intersect,
  3. Infinite solutions: equations represent the same straight line.

This generalises to any number of equations in any number of unknowns.

Lines, planes and equations

  1. How many points is needed to define a straight line?
  2. How many equations is needed to define a straight line in 2D?
  3. How many points is needed to define a plane?
  4. How many equations is needed to define a plane in 2D?
  5. How many equations is needed to define a straight line in 3D?
  1. two points, 2) one equation, 3) three points, 4) one equation, 5) two equations defining the intersection of two planes.

Vectors

  • A vector is a half-line, arrow, or ray,

  • Can be thought of as an infitily, infinitely thin line, like a light ray.

  • Starts at the origin \((0,0,\ldots,0)\)

  • Defined by its magnitude (how long the arrow is),

  • and direction (angle the line makes with a fixed, usually horizontal axis).

  • Vectors work in any dimension.

Representations

  • Depending on how we want to use them, we can represent vectors in many different ways.

  • Cartesian Co-ordinates: an ordered tuple \((x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) representing the co-ordinate values

  • Polar Co-ordinates: \((r, \theta)\), where \(r\) is the length and \(\theta\) is the anticlockwise angle with the \(x\)-axis.

  • Using a basis: \(x \mathbf{i} + y \mathbf{j}\), where \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) are unit vectors pointing along the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axex.

Cartesian

The one we all know and love from primary school.

\((3, 4)\) – three along, four up.

Adding Vectors

To add vectors \(\mathbf{u} = \pmatrix{u_1 \\ u_2\\} = \pmatrix{3 \\ 4}\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \pmatrix{v_1 \\ v_2} = \pmatrix{2 \\ -1}\),

We add their components \[ \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}3+2\\ 4+-1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \]

Adding vectors

To graphically add \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\)…

Attach the tail of \(\mathbf{v}\) to the head of \(\mathbf{u}\), the head of \(\mathbf{v}\) points to \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\).

Scaling vectors

Multiply a vector \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}\) by a number \(m = 3/2\).

Multiply each component of \(\mathbf{u}\) by \(m\): \[ m\cdot\mathbf{u}=\frac{3}{2}\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 4 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}9/2\\ 6 \end{pmatrix} \]

Graphically, multiplies the length by \(3\), but doesn’t change its direction.

Distance

How far apart are \(\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}\)

We need to find the distance between \((3,4)\) and \((2, -1)\).

We know that \(3\) and \(2\) are one square apart, and \(4\) and \(-1\) are five squares apart.

Now we can use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the distance: \[ d^2 = 1^2 + 5^2 = 26 \Longrightarrow d = \sqrt{26}. \]

  • It turns out that Pythagoras’ theorem works in higher dimensions…

  • I.e., if we have two vectors \(\mathbf{u} = (u_1,\ldots,u_n)\) and \(\mathbf{v} = (v_1,\ldots,v_n)\),

  • Then we calculate their distance as

    \(\sqrt{ (v_1 - u_1)^2 + (v_2 - u_2)^2 + \cdots + (v^n - u^n)^2 }\)

  • See also [https://youtu.be/mceaM2_zQd8]

Dot product

Lets you find the angle between two vectors: \(\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}, \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}\).

  • \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1 \times v_1 + u_2 \times v_2 + \cdots u_n \times v_n\).
  • $(3, 4) (2, -1) = 3 + 4
  • \((3, 4) \cdot (2, -1) = 12 + -4 = 8\)

  • More precisely, \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}\) gives us the product of the length of \(\mathbf{u}\), length of \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\cos(\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is the angle of separation between \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\).

  • Why might you want this?

    • Remember that \(\cos(90^\circ) = \cos(\pi / 2) = 0\)…
    • we can tell if two vectors are perpendicular if their dot product is \(0\).
    • we can also tell whether the angle is accute or obtuce.
    • many applications in physics, graphics, …

Quick note

  • Take care that the vectors you are adding / multiplying / finding the distance / computing the dot product are compatible.

  • I.e., these operations only work if vectors have the same number of components.

What’s the point, anyway?

  • Computer graphics and vision
    • Games – animation and movement, rendering 3d models on a 2d screen
  • Machine learning
    • Multiple features of data can be stored as a vector.
  • Civil, electrical and mechanical engineering
  • Physics – build mathematical modelss of the world using quantum mechanics

In conclusion, it’s a simple (mathematically straightforward and computationally efficient) way of modelling lots of real-world phenomena.

Vector Bases

  • We can define a vector as a linear combination of basis vectors

  • Remember when we scaled a vector (multiplied a vector by a number)?

    \(m \cdot \mathbf{u} = (m u_1, m u_2, \ldots m u_n)\)

  • The number \(m\) is called a scalar.

Vector vs Scalar

  • The simplest definition of vector is

    “Quantity which cannot be represented by a single number.”

  • A scalar is a quantity which can be represented by a single number.

Scalar Vector
Distance \(3.2m\) Displacement \(3.2m\) east
Speed \(340.29m/s\) Velocity \(1.2 m/s\) downwards
Mass \(60kg\) Force \(600 N\) upwards
Time \(7s\)
Electric field \(100 N/C\) to the right

Vector Bases

  • We can scale a vector by multiplying it by a number.

    • E.g., in 2d, if we have \(\mathbf{x} = (1,0)\) we can reach any point on the \(x\)-axis by scaling \(\mathbf{x}\).

  • But we cannot get to any place on the plane where \(y \ne 0\).

  • To do this, we add another vector \(\mathbf{y} = (0,1)\).

    • We can scale \((0,1)\) to reach any point on the \(y\)-axis.

  • Now we can reach any point on the grid by adding a multiple of \(\mathbf{x}\) to a multiple of \(\mathbf{y}\).

    \(a \mathbf{x} = b \mathbf{y}\)

  • \(\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}\) is called a basis for the 2-dimensional plane.

Other bases for the same space

We can generate any point on the plane with

  • \((1, 0), (0,2)\) (scaled)
  • \((1, 0), (1, 2)\) (skewed)
  • \((1, 1), (1, -1)\) (rotate)

But why? It allows us to look at things from a different perspective.

Our calculations might be easier in a different basis, and we can even perform non-linear transformations if we need that for our model.

Linear transformations

  • We can send points from one vector space to another using a linear transformation – a mathematical function which takes a vector and returns a vector.

    A linear map:

    1. Preserves the origin: \((0, 0, \ldots, 0)\) always maps to \((0,0, \ldots, 0)\)
    2. Preserves straight lines: straight lines in the input space remain straight in the output space.

    In other words, grid-lines remain straight and evenly spaced.

Linear transformations

  • There are also affine maps, which allow translation (origin doesn’t have to map to origin)

  • Linear / affine maps can

    • change dimension, e.g., project from \(3\) to \(2\)-dimensional space.
    • be reversible or irreversible. e.g., a reflection, rotation, scale or skew can be undone, but a projection cannot.

Linear maps

Formally, a linear map is a function \[ \begin{align*} f& : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k\\ f&(\mathbf{x}) = A \mathbf{x} \end{align*} \]

where

  • \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the input vector space (\(n\)-dimensional vectors),
  • \(\mathbb{R}^k\) is the output vector space (\(k\)-dimensional vectors),
  • \(\mathbf{x}\) is the input vector (\(n\) elements)
  • \(A\) is a transformation matrix, an \((n \times k)\)-matrix which performs the linear transformation
  • \(f(\mathbf{x})\) is the \(k\)-dimensional output vector

Matrices

  • A matrix is a rectangular table of values \[ \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \ldots & a_{1n}\\ a_{21} & a_{22} & \ldots & a_{2n}\\ & & \vdots & \\ a_{k1} & a_{k2} & \ldots & a_{kn}\\ \end{pmatrix} \]
  • It has \(k\) rows, \(n\) columns – we write \((k \times n)\).
  • Matrices are powerful tools, and operations such as addition, multiplication are defined.
  • Special matrix operations like determinant and tensor product are also defined, but that’s a conversation for another day.

Matrix multiplied by vector

  • There is an algorithm for general matrix multiplication, and you can do it by hand.
  • However, computers can do it quickly and accurately.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \ldots & a_{1n}\\ a_{21} & a_{22} & \ldots & a_{2n}\\ & & \vdots & \\ a_{k1} & a_{k2} & \ldots & a_{kn}\\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ \vdots \\ b_n \end{pmatrix} =\)
  • \(\begin{pmatrix} a_{11} b_1 + a_{12} + \ldots + a_{1n} b_n\\ a_{21} b_1 + a_{22} + \ldots + a_{2n} b_n\\ \vdots \\ a_{k1} b_1 + a_{k2} b_2 + \ldots + a_{kn} b_n\\ \end{pmatrix}\)

Back to our linear map

Formally, a linear map is a function \[ \begin{align*} f& : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k\\ f& (\mathbf{x}) = A \mathbf{x} \end{align*} \]

  • The matrix \(A\) applies some kind of transformation to each component of the input \(\mathbf{x}\).
  • The dimension of the matrix determines the size of the output and whether the map is one-to-one or not.
  • Enough formality, how do we actually build one?

see notes

Process: we start with the standard basis \((1,0), (0,1)\), then we figure out what the transformation does to this basis. In our example, we see that \((1,0)\) goes to \((3,1)\), and \((0,1)\) goes to \((1,2)\). These new basis vectors become the columns of our linear transformation.

This one reflects the cube about the line \(y = -x\) and doubles its size. Figure out the linear transformation matrix.

Space calculations

  • Vectors represent infinitely long lines with no width: an excellent model for a ray of light.
  • However, space is curved, so light curves as it moves through space.
  • We can model this using a linear map.

  • But wait, I hear you cry, shouldn’t linear maps preserve straight lines?

    Yes… ah nevermind, it was only me who got upset by that part.

  • It’s alright, we can still use a smooth map to model this transformation, and for our purposes, they work much the same!

Warping of space

  • We can think of space as being distorted by a series of equal waves.
  • These waves follow a sinusoidal pattern.

We can transform a straight line into a sin wave by multiplying the \(x\)-value by \(\sin\).

Vectors and information retrieval

The vector space model is one of the simplest information retrieval mechanisms.

Terminology

  • Document: collection of words
    • We write \(\mathbf{d}_1, \mathbf{d}_2, \ldots\) and refer to them by number \(i\).
  • Query a word or sequence of words, \(\mathbf{q}\)
    • Our search term
  • Relevance / Similarity
    • A measure of how closely our query matches a particular document,
    • Defined as the distance between \(\mathbf{q}\) and a document \(\mathbf{d}_i\).
    • Formally, we can write \(\Vert \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{d}_i \Vert\)

Document analysis

In 3d space, we have three axes

Each axis represents a subject

  • \(x\)-axis represents Bath Spa,
  • \(y\)-axis represents Romans,
  • \(z\)-axis represents Computing.

E.g., a document all about Romans, would lie along the \(y\)-axis.

Document analysis

  • Example: a document about Romans and Bath spa,

  • Lies somewhere between the \(x\) and \(y\) axis.

  • And should not point in the \(z\) direction (for computing) at all.

  • E.g., \((2, 1, 0)\)

In the example (2,1) the document mentions Bath Spa twice as often as it mentions Romans, and mentions Computing not at all.

Document analysis

  • Example: a document mentioning Computing and Bath Spa,

  • Lies somewhere between the \(x\) and \(z\) axis.

  • And should not point in the \(y\) direction (for Romans) at all.

  • E.g., \((3, 0, 2)\)

In this case, we can guess that, for every three times Bath Spa is mentioned, Computing is mentioned twice.

Search query

  • Suppose someone wants to find out about the Computing course at Bath Spa University

  • The vector \(\mathbf{q} = (1,0,1)\) is our query.

  • We search for the document which is closest to \(\mathbf{q}\)

Closest Calculation

Earlier we worked out the distance between two vectors…

  • Using Pythagoras’ theorem, extended to 3D.

    • With query \(\mathbf{q} = (q_1, q_2, q_3) = (1, 0, 1)\),

    • For each document \(\mathbf{d}_i = (d_{i1}, d_{i2}, d_{i3})\),

    • Calculate \(\sqrt{(d_{i1} - q_1)^2 + (d_{i2} - q_2)^2 + (d_{i3} - q_3)^2}\).

    • Then choose the document with minimum distance

    • Since we only care about relative distances, we can forget about the square root.

Extending to higher dimensions

  • If we had more categories, we could construct a model in a higher-dimensional vector space

    • Harder to draw, but just as straightforward to work with (in a computer).

  • If we have \(n = 42\) possible document categories, we can represent each document as a \(42\)-dimensional vector:

    \((d_{i1},d_{i2},d_{i3},\ldots,d_{i41},d_{i42})\)

  • A query is also a \(42\)-dimensional vector, and we calculate the squared distance in the same way:

    \((d_{i1} - q_1)^2 + (d_{i2} - q_2)^2 + (d_{i3} - q_3)^2 + \cdots + (d_{in} - q_n)^2\)

TF-IDF

TF-IDF

  • Term Frequency, Inverse Document Frequency

  • Search / information retrieval algorithm

  • Gives a measure of importance of a word to a document, corrected for the fact that some words are more common than others.

  • Simple but powerful model, widely used in, e.g., academic library search.

Bag of words

  • We have \(n\) search terms, and each document will be represented by an \(n\)-vector

  • Component \(i\) of the vector represents the weighting of the document to category \(i\).

For example

We have three documents:

  1. Tak does not require that we think of Him, only that we think
  2. The first thing Tak did, he wrote himself.
  3. Logic is a wonderful thing but doesn’t always beat actual thought.

Bag Of Words

  1. Tak does not require that we think of Him, only that we think
{
    "tak": 1,
    "does": 1,
    "not": 1,
    "require": 1,
    "that": 2,
    "we": 2,
    "think": 2,
    "of": 1,
    "him": 1,
    "only": 1
}

total_words = 13

Term Frequency

\[ \text{Term frequency of } w = \dfrac{\text{occurances of word } w}{\text{total words in document}} \]

For example,

  • “Tak” occurs once in \(d_1\),

    \(\mathrm{Tf}(\text{"Tak"}, D_1) = \dfrac{1}{13}\)

  • “Think” occurs twice in \(d_1\),

    \(\mathrm{Tf}(\text{"Think"}, D_1) = \dfrac{2}{13}\)

Inverse document frequency

  • Term frequency gives us a measure of how common a word is,

  • Inverse document frequency corrects for the distribution of words in our set of documents.

  • E.g., in a set of Dracula quotes, the word “blood” is likely to appear often, so it should be less important than less common words, like “paprika”.

Inverse Document Frequency

\[ \text{inverse document frequency } w = \dfrac{\text{total number of documents}}{\text{number of documents containing } w} \]

  1. Tak does not require that we think of Him, only that we think
  2. The first thing Tak did, he wrote himself.
  3. Logic is a wonderful thing but doesn’t always beat actual thought.

Examples:

  • The word “Tak” occurs in two out of three documents

    \(\mathrm{Idf}(\text{"Tak"}, D) = \dfrac{3}{2}\)

  • The word “logic” occurs in one out of three documents

    \(\mathrm{Idf}(\text{"Tak"}, D) = \dfrac{3}{1}\)

  • Often we take the logarithm of IDF to adjust the scale.
